basis: spiritual drink from the rock interpreted as Christ
note: Paul identifies Israel's water-giving rock with Christ. This Christian reading brings the commentary's rock-and-water image into a specific typological tradition rather than treating it as a generic well motif.

basis: perishable body raised imperishable
note: The resurrection is sown perishable and raised imperishable, placing the commentary's language of permanence in a bodily Christian eschatological setting.

basis: fire tests each one's work
note: The commentary's metal foam separates from useful material, and its later image distinguishes what vanishes from what remains; Paul says fire tests the quality of each person's work, giving that separation an explicit judgment setting.

basis: work that remains receives reward
note: The commentary says the hereafter is more abiding and that foam goes while what benefits remains; Paul says the builder whose work remains receives a reward, linking endurance to evaluated work.

basis: burned work means loss
note: The commentary casts the residue as what goes and is not counted; Paul says burned work brings loss, the contrary outcome to work that survives the fire.

basis: work burned and its maker suffers loss
note: In the fire-test of works, what burns is lost. Alongside the commentary's metal-smelting foam, it supplies a Christian judgment image where material does not endure the furnace.

basis: hidden motives brought to light
note: The commentary says God knows what is hidden; Paul says the Lord will bring hidden things to light and disclose heart's purposes, specifying hidden human motives as the object of that knowledge.

basis: world passes; God's will remains
note: The commentary contrasts vanishing foam with the more abiding hereafter; 1 John says the world and its desire pass away while the one doing God's will remains forever, giving the contrast an ethical criterion.

basis: world passes away; God-doer remains forever
note: The world and its desire pass away while the one doing God's will remains forever. It gives a concise ethical form to the commentary's passing-versus-abiding contrast.

basis: all human glory like grass
note: The commentary's dried pasture becomes residue that disperses; Peter quotes Isaiah's grass and flower image for all flesh and human glory, extending the fading-vegetation picture to human life.

basis: grass withers and flower falls
note: Peter applies the grass-and-flower image to mortal flesh; it gives a close Christian counterpart to the commentary's pasture becoming transient debris.

basis: word of the Lord remains forever
note: The commentary pairs beneficial reminder with an abiding hereafter; Peter quotes the grass that withers and then says the Lord's word remains forever, applying Isaiah's transience contrast to the proclaimed good news.

basis: word remains forever
note: The verse makes the preached word enduring after the preceding grass has withered, a direct analogue for the reminder whose benefit outlasts what goes away.

basis: imperishable heavenly inheritance
note: The commentary says the hereafter is better and more abiding; 1 Peter describes an inheritance kept in heaven as imperishable, undefiled, and unfading, specifying what such permanence means.

basis: faith tested as gold by fire
note: The commentary invokes metal melted for useful things and contrasts transient residue with lasting good; Peter compares tested faith to gold refined by fire and locates its result at Jesus' appearing.

basis: perishable gold tested by fire and proven faith
note: Peter calls even fire-tested gold perishable while faith is proved through trial, a carefully different but relevant interpretation of the commentary's molten-metal image and its question of what endures.

basis: few saved through flood water
note: Peter's flood reference makes water the medium through which a few are preserved rather than merely a current that carries refuse away. That reversal gives the commentary's flood image a distinct Christian eschatological reading.

basis: flood water interpreted through baptism and a good conscience
note: The next verse interprets the flood-water figure as baptism, expressly denying a merely bodily washing and locating its benefit in an appeal to God through resurrection.

basis: piety useful now and for the coming life
note: Piety is called beneficial and is said to promise life both now and in the future. The verse tightly pairs the commentary's benefit vocabulary with its final-life horizon.

basis: seen is transient; unseen is eternal
note: The commentary pairs God's knowledge of what is public and hidden with a more abiding hereafter; Paul contrasts visible transient things with unseen eternal things, bringing hiddenness and permanence together.

basis: visible temporary and invisible eternal
note: Paul explicitly contrasts the temporary seen realm with the eternal unseen one, a close Pauline formulation of the commentary's final better-and-more-enduring horizon.

basis: destroyed earthly dwelling and eternal heavenly dwelling
note: Paul contrasts the destructible earthly tent with an eternal dwelling from God. It gives the commentary's better, more enduring hereafter a concrete dwelling-place form.

basis: waterless springs and storm-driven mists as false teachers
note: False teachers are waterless springs and mists driven by a storm. The deliberately unhelpful water image gives a sharp inverse to the commentary's reminder that must benefit and water that truly remains.

basis: Scripture is profitable for instruction
note: The commentary asks whether a reminder benefits and defines benefit by help toward good; Paul describes Scripture as useful for teaching, reproof, correction, and training in righteousness, a direct Christian account of beneficial instruction.

basis: Scripture useful for teaching, correction, and training
note: Scripture is explicitly useful for teaching and correction, a precise Christian formulation of admonition whose value lies in actually helping its recipient.

basis: equipped for every good work
note: The commentary links benefit to reaching good and the hereafter to what is better; Paul says Scripture equips the person of God for every good work, identifying the practical result of useful instruction.

basis: washing of water with the word
note: Ephesians explicitly joins cleansing water to the word, a close Christian analogue to the commentary's clear well and reminder that does good.

basis: sowing to decay or to eternal life
note: Paul contrasts a harvest of corruption from flesh with eternal life from the Spirit. The agricultural separation adds a Christian ethical form to the commentary's perishing residue and abiding good.

basis: better and abiding possession
note: The commentary describes the hereafter as better and more abiding; Hebrews says its addressees know they possess a better and abiding possession, a close formulation of the same contrast in a persecution context.

basis: shaken things removed; unshaken things remain
note: The commentary's foam goes while water remains and calls the hereafter more abiding; Hebrews says what can be shaken is removed so that what cannot be shaken remains, making permanence the outcome of divine judgment.

basis: shaken things removed so unshakable things remain
note: Hebrews reads cosmic shaking as removal of what can be shaken so that what cannot be shaken may remain, an eschatological counterpart to separating passing surface matter from what stays.

basis: no lasting city here and a future city sought
note: Hebrews explicitly denies a lasting city in the present and directs attention to the one to come, closely matching the commentary's contrast between what goes and the more abiding final reality.

basis: message heard but not benefiting its hearers
note: Hebrews says that a proclaimed message did not benefit some hearers because it was not joined to faith. It is an unusually exact Christian counterpoint to the commentary's conditional, benefit-bearing reminder.

basis: rain yields a useful crop
note: The commentary defines benefit as what helps attain good and sets retained water against useless residue; Hebrews pictures ground drinking repeated rain and producing a useful crop, explicitly joining water with benefit.

basis: land drinks rain and yields useful vegetation
note: Land that drinks repeated rain and bears a crop useful to its cultivators receives blessing. Its exact useful-water logic closely mirrors the commentary's water that remains and benefits people.

basis: thorns rejected and burned
note: The commentary's dried plant matter becomes flood refuse that goes away; Hebrews contrasts useful crop with land bearing thorns and thistles, rejected and ending in fire, giving the unproductive growth an ethical and judgmental outcome.

basis: thorns prove worthless and end in burning
note: The same field image sets useful rain-fed growth against worthless thorns whose end is burning, adding a Christian antithesis to the commentary's residue versus what is discarded.

basis: flower fades and rich man withers
note: The commentary calls the plant residue dried and passing; James likens the rich person to a flower that withers under scorching heat, applying the fading-plant image to worldly prosperity.

basis: scorched grass and fallen flower
note: James describes sun-scorched grass, a fallen flower, and fading beauty; it closely echoes the commentary's pasture that becomes dry, transient matter.

basis: wave driven and tossed by wind
note: The doubter is a sea-wave driven by wind, a specific instability image that helps mark why the commentary values what settles, remains, and can benefit.

basis: one spring cannot yield fresh and bitter water
note: The commentary's source gloss describes cleaning a well until clear water appears, and it presents reminder as speech that may benefit; James uses spring-water quality to test speech, asking whether one opening can yield both fresh and bitter water.

basis: one spring cannot issue fresh and bitter water
note: James uses a spring's water quality to test speech, giving the commentary's clear well an ethical and verbal extension rather than a merely physical one.

basis: water springing up to eternal life
note: The commentary connects water held in rock hollows with the hereafter's greater permanence; Jesus says the water he gives becomes a spring welling up to eternal life, joining water's benefit to enduring life.

basis: water becomes a spring into eternal life
note: Jesus' water becomes an inner spring that wells into eternal life, bringing together well water, benefit, and the enduring final life named in the commentary.

basis: perishing food and food enduring to eternal life
note: Jesus contrasts food that perishes with food enduring to eternal life, directly joining utility, perishing, and the permanent life foregrounded by the commentary.

basis: flowing rivers of living water
note: The believer is promised flowing living water; it develops the commentary's life-bearing abundance beyond water merely trapped in a well or hollow.

basis: living-water image explained as the Spirit
note: The narrator identifies the preceding rivers of living water with the Spirit, giving an internal Christian interpretation that prevents the water image from being read as only physical supply.

basis: waterless clouds carried by winds and fruitless uprooted trees
note: Jude's false teachers promise water but carry none and are wind-driven, fruitless trees. This combines empty water, dispersal, and failed vegetation against the commentary's useful retained water.

basis: wheat gathered; chaff burned
note: The commentary's غثاء is plant residue that disperses and counts for nothing; John gathers wheat into the barn and burns the chaff, making agricultural separation a judgment image of what is kept and what is discarded.

basis: digging deep to rock; flood cannot shake the house
note: The hearer who acts digs deep, founds on rock, and withstands a flood. This is a particularly close meeting of useful admonition, a worked depth in rock, and endurance under rushing water.

basis: word held fast and bearing fruit
note: The commentary makes reminder beneficial only where it helps toward good and compares it to water held in hollows; Luke's good soil hears the word, holds it fast, and bears fruit with patience, giving reception and retention an ethical outcome.

basis: passing heaven and earth; imperishable words
note: Jesus contrasts the passing of heaven and earth with words that will not pass, a direct word-level counterpart to the commentary's contrast between what goes away and what is more lasting.

basis: earthly treasure is destroyed or stolen
note: The commentary's foam is what goes while beneficial value remains; Jesus names moth, rust, and thieves as agents that remove earthly treasure, supplying concrete forms of worldly loss against the heavenly treasure in the next verse.

basis: treasure in heaven does not decay
note: The commentary says the hereafter is better and more abiding than the transient; Jesus contrasts earthly loss with treasure in heaven that moth and rust cannot consume, making durability a reason to value the future.

basis: treasure immune to decay and theft
note: Treasure in heaven avoids moth, corrosion, and theft, a concrete Jesus tradition for valuing what lasts over what is consumed or lost.

basis: the Father sees what is done secretly
note: The commentary says God knows what is public and hidden; Jesus says the Father who sees what is done in secret will reward, adding a moral consequence to divine knowledge of concealed acts.

basis: hearing and doing; rock foundation
note: The commentary compares a beneficial reminder to water held in created rock hollows; Jesus says the one who hears and does his words is like a house built on rock, joining received teaching to stability.

basis: rain and flood test the rock house
note: The commentary sets water that stays against foam and debris that wash away; Matthew's rain, floods, and winds batter the rock-founded house without bringing it down, making endurance under water the result of doing the teaching.

basis: rain and flood collapse the sand house
note: The commentary contrasts water retained with transient residue; Matthew's rain and floods collapse the house built on sand, the contrary outcome when the teaching is heard but not done.

basis: water of life freely given to the thirsty
note: The enthroned speaker gives life-water freely to the thirsty in the new creation, an explicit final-state counterpart to water as what truly benefits and remains.

basis: river of the water of life
note: The commentary links water gathered and retained with the lasting hereafter; Revelation's final-city vision has the river of the water of life flowing from God's throne, making life-giving water an eschatological provision.

basis: river of water of life from God's throne
note: The final vision's pure river of life flowing from God's throne gives an eschatological culmination to the commentary's contrast between passing surface matter and life-bearing water.

basis: fruit and leaves for healing
note: The commentary defines benefit as help toward good and sets it beside the abiding hereafter; Revelation's tree by the river bears fruit and leaves for the healing of nations, giving the final water scene a concrete benefit.

basis: perpetual fruit and healing leaves by life-water
note: The tree beside the life-river bears fruit continually and heals nations, developing the water's durable public benefit beyond the commentary's immediate flood scene.

basis: Lamb guides to springs of life-water
note: The Lamb guides the afflicted to springs of life-water and removes tears. This eschatological pastoral use of water sharpens the commentary's claim that the final state is better and enduring.

basis: inexhaustible fountain of righteousness and springs of wisdom
note: The thirsty drink from an inexhaustible fountain and are filled with wisdom; it makes abundant water a specific image for wisdom that benefits and does not run out.

basis: resurrection to lasting life
note: The commentary says the hereafter is better and more abiding; the martyr in 2 Maccabees expects the King of the world to raise the dead to renewed life, placing endurance in bodily resurrection rather than present survival.

basis: resurrection to everlasting renewal of life
note: The martyr contrasts present death with the world's King's everlasting renewal. It supplies a Second Temple Jewish formulation of the commentary's claim that the final life is better and more lasting.

basis: ever-strengthening spring and unceasing river
note: Study for its own sake makes a person like an ever-strengthening spring and a river that does not cease, an interpretive expansion of beneficial instruction into enduring water.

basis: water drops wear stone; Torah study
note: The commentary imagines rain held in a rock hollow and a beneficial reminder as retained water; Rabbi Akiva's story has drops wear a stone and prompt him to begin Torah study, turning the rock-water meeting into an image of instruction's effect rather than storage.

basis: water interpreted as Torah and recurring public reading
note: The Bavli reads Israel's three waterless days as three days without Torah and grounds regular Torah reading in that image. It gives the commentary's beneficial reminder a concrete water-and-remembrance practice.

basis: plastered cistern that loses not a drop
note: The saying praises Rabbi Eliezer's retention of teaching as a cistern that loses no water. It turns the commentary's held water into a precise Jewish image of durable remembrance.

basis: Wisdom as a canal from a river into a garden
note: Personified Wisdom describes herself as a canal from a river entering a garden. The scene makes instruction's water a deliberately directed supply rather than passing flood debris.

basis: teaching poured out for future generations
note: In the same water-and-Wisdom sequence, teaching is poured out and left for generations to come. It adds explicit transmission and duration to the commentary's useful reminder and what remains.

basis: Torah compared to descending water
note: The commentary makes the benefit of a reminder depend on its helping people reach good and imagines water gathered in hollows; Ta'anit 7a compares Torah to water that descends from high places to low and says Torah endures in the humble, giving receptivity a rabbinic interpretation.

basis: Torah likened to water that descends to low places
note: The Bavli's water-Torah comparison adds humility to the commentary's teaching-as-water connection: water leaves high places for low ones, as Torah is received by the humble.

basis: healed spring water
note: The commentary cites cleaning a well until clear water appears; Elisha goes to Jericho's source and heals its water, so the unusable source becomes sound, a narrative counterpart to water cleared for use.

basis: bad water healed so death and barrenness cease
note: Elisha heals a city's bad water, ending its deadly effect. This gives a narrative extension to the commentary's water made clear and useful rather than left covered or corrupt.

basis: valley made full of ditches
note: The command to fill a wadi with excavated ditches is a close scene-parallel to the commentary's winding low-lying hollows prepared to receive water.

basis: water filling the wadi and its pits
note: Water fills the excavated valley despite the absence of visible rain or wind, extending the preceding ditch scene into an image of water retained in depressions.

basis: everlasting life
note: The commentary calls the hereafter better and more abiding than worldly life; Daniel's resurrection scene distinguishes everlasting life from disgrace, giving a concrete scriptural account of the lasting afterlife.

basis: awakening to everlasting life
note: Daniel's resurrection scene distinguishes everlasting life from everlasting contempt, giving a Hebrew Bible eschatological analogue for the more enduring hereafter.

basis: teaching falls as rain
note: The commentary says a reminder may benefit and defines benefit as help toward good; Moses describes his teaching as rain and dew, making instruction itself life-giving water.

basis: teaching as rain and speech as dew
note: Moses explicitly casts teaching and speech as rain and dew on vegetation, a direct bridge between beneficial admonition and the commentary's water imagery.

basis: streams, fountains, and depths in valleys and hills
note: The promised land is characterized by plentiful water emerging through valleys and hills. It gives a land-scale counterpart to the commentary's wells, hollows, and flood-filled low places.

basis: secret deeds judged
note: The commentary says God knows what is public and what is hidden; Ecclesiastes says God brings every deed, including every hidden thing, into judgment, adding the ethical consequence of divine knowledge.

basis: God's work endures
note: The commentary moves from God creating and ordering water-holding rock to the hereafter being more abiding; Ecclesiastes says whatever God does endures forever, directly joining divine action and permanence.

basis: what God does endures
note: Ecclesiastes says that what God does endures and cannot be altered, a compact counterpart to the commentary's definition of remaining in one's original state against annihilation.

basis: water from rock for a thirsty people
note: Water comes from a rock and the people drink. Unlike a lexical comparison, the shared scene joins rock, abundant water, and direct human benefit that the commentary develops across its word-families.

basis: Israel called silver dross
note: The commentary distinguishes useless metal foam from the useful metal that remains; Ezekiel calls the house of Israel silver dross in a furnace, reversing the comparison so the community itself is the refuse to be judged.

basis: remaining water fouled by trampling
note: The powerful sheep foul the water left for others. This ethical inversion of clean, beneficial water adds a social consequence to the commentary's insistence that what remains should benefit people.

basis: clean water removes impurity
note: The commentary's muddy well is cleaned until clear water appears; Ezekiel promises clean water that cleanses Israel from uncleanness, extending the well-clearing image to covenant restoration.

basis: clean water removes uncleanness
note: Ezekiel's sprinkling of clean water makes cleansing the point of the water image, an explicit interpretive bridge to the commentary's purified, visible well-water.

basis: river-fed trees; food and healing
note: The commentary defines benefit as help toward good and describes rain held in rock pools; Ezekiel's river nourishes trees whose fruit feeds and leaves heal, making the water's benefit concrete in an eschatological landscape.

basis: perennial fruit and healing leaves by the river
note: River-fed trees bear new fruit continually and have healing leaves, developing the lasting-benefit side that the commentary distributes between water, usefulness, and endurance.

basis: water wherever the river goes gives life
note: Ezekiel's river makes living creatures live wherever it reaches, an expansive counterpart to water as the useful residue rather than the discarded surface matter.

basis: waters gathered into one place
note: The commentary's rock hollows and its explanation of abundant water as water gathered both stress collected water; Genesis makes gathering the waters an act of creation, showing such pools within a larger scriptural ordering of water.

basis: waters gathered into one place
note: Creation begins with waters being gathered so dry land can appear. This is a direct counterpart to the commentary's note that abundant water is named for its gathering, while retaining the creation setting.

basis: wells stopped and filled with earth
note: The Philistines block Abraham's wells with earth, the physical inverse of the commentary's well cleared of covering mud so its water can be seen and used.

basis: Isaac reopens the stopped wells
note: Isaac digs again the wells that had been stopped. The recovery of usable water supplies a narrative continuation for the commentary's action of clearing a well until its water reappears.

basis: well of living water found in a valley
note: Isaac's servants find living water while digging in a valley, closely bringing together the commentary's low-lying hollows, plentiful well, and water that can be retained for life.

basis: dew vanishes; chaff scatters
note: The commentary calls flood-borne plant matter residue that goes away; Hosea compares idolatrous Ephraim to dew that vanishes and chaff swept from the threshing floor, adding transient moisture to the disappearing residue image.

basis: dew, chaff, and smoke driven away
note: Hosea layers quickly disappearing dew with wind-driven chaff and smoke, an unusually close biblical cluster for the commentary's floatable debris that is scattered and gone.

basis: silver become dross and wine diluted with water
note: Isaiah puts debased silver and weakened water in one moral image. Its deliberate dross-and-water pairing is a close biblical companion to the commentary's two-sided flood-and-metal surface waste.

basis: dross smelted from Zion
note: The commentary includes foam separating from molten metal while useful metal remains; Isaiah's refiner removes Zion's dross and alloy, applying metal separation to the city's moral purification.

basis: God smelts away dross and removes alloy
note: God's restorative judgment removes dross from Jerusalem. It gives the commentary's furnace residue a moral purification setting in which what corrupts is taken away so that a renewed community remains.

basis: drawing water from wells of salvation
note: The joyful drawing of water from salvation's wells turns stored well-water into a salvation image, complementing the commentary's claim that retained water helps one reach the good.

basis: roaring waters and fleeing chaff
note: The commentary joins flood-borne residue to water that remains; Isaiah depicts roaring nations rebuked and chased like chaff before wind, bringing the water-and-disappearing-residue images together in a judgment scene.

basis: roaring waters answered by wind-driven chaff
note: Nations roar like many waters yet flee at rebuke like chaff before the wind. The verse unusually joins a water figure to dispersed chaff, close to the commentary's flood and unreckoned debris.

basis: reservoir for old-pool water and its maker
note: Isaiah names a built reservoir holding former-pool water but rebukes those who do not look to its Maker. It sets human water engineering beside the commentary's created rock cavities and keeps the Creator relation in view.

basis: waters measured by the Creator
note: The commentary links its measured wadis to created rock hollows that collect rain; Isaiah asks who measured the waters and marked off the heavens, placing water's bounded order under the Creator's measure.

basis: all flesh is grass
note: The commentary's dried plant residue belongs to the cycle of pasture becoming waste; Isaiah begins its grass-and-flower comparison by declaring all flesh grass, extending that transience from vegetation to human life.

basis: grass and flower wither
note: The commentary identifies غثاء as dried vegetation carried off by a flood; Isaiah's grass and flower wither, portraying created vitality as transient and preparing the contrast with what endures.

basis: God's word stands forever
note: The commentary pairs a reminder that benefits with the hereafter as more abiding; Isaiah says the grass fades but God's word stands forever, giving divine speech the permanence absent from the residue.

basis: withered grass and the word that stands
note: Isaiah places fading grass and flower beside God's word that stands forever, joining this commentary's dry pasture and vanishing refuse to its useful reminder and abiding side.

basis: springs in valleys and pools in dry land
note: God opens fountains in valleys and makes pools and springs in dry country; the verse directly gathers the commentary's hollows, low places, and life-preserving water.

basis: rain waters the earth
note: The commentary describes sky-water collected in hollows and links water's benefit to good; Isaiah's rain waters the earth and makes it bring forth seed and bread, supplying the agricultural effect behind its water-and-benefit comparison.

basis: rain watering earth for seed and bread
note: Rain descends and makes the earth produce food; this is the productive-water half of the commentary's comparison between retained water and a reminder that benefits.

basis: rain-like word accomplishes its purpose
note: The commentary joins stored water to a reminder that may help people reach good; Isaiah compares God's effective word to rain, saying it does not return empty but accomplishes its purpose, an explicit scriptural bridge from water to beneficial speech.

basis: word accomplishing its purpose
note: Isaiah's following word-image says God's utterance does not return empty but accomplishes its purpose, supplying a textual model for speech evaluated by its benefit rather than its surface appearance.

basis: restless sea casts up mire
note: The commentary's flood carries surface debris that disperses; Isaiah's restless sea casts up mire and mud and cannot rest, using the water's refuse as an image of the wicked, while the surah's foam is what the current leaves behind.

basis: restless sea casting up mire and dirt
note: Isaiah's restless sea throws mire and dirt onto its surface, the negative inverse of the commentary's well cleared of mud so that water can appear clear.

basis: watered garden and unfailing spring
note: Divine guidance yields a watered garden and a spring whose waters do not fail, a concentrated counterpart to water that stays, aids people, and is more lasting.

basis: tree beside water survives heat
note: The commentary sets dried pasture against water gathered in hollows; Jeremiah's tree sends roots to water, keeps green leaves through heat and drought, and continues bearing fruit, giving rooted endurance a distinct trust-and-drought setting.

basis: rooted tree remains green and fruitful by water
note: A tree stretching roots to a stream does not fear heat or cease bearing fruit. It provides the durable, useful counterpoint to vegetation that becomes scattered and gone.

basis: living fountain and broken cisterns
note: The commentary's created rock hollows retain sky-water while flood foam disperses; Jeremiah contrasts the fountain of living water with cisterns unable to hold water, making failed retention an explicit counter-image.

basis: living fountain and broken cisterns
note: Jeremiah contrasts God as a source of living water with human-cut cisterns that cannot retain water. Its failure of retention reverses the commentary's God-created rock hollows that hold sky water, making the contrast instructive.

basis: refining goes on in vain because wickedness is not removed
note: Jeremiah describes a failed furnace process: the fire works but the evil is not separated. It is a pointed inverse to the commentary's clean division in which the useless surface matter actually goes away.

basis: water wears stone and washes soil
note: The commentary describes rock hollows holding rain and flood matter dispersing; Job reverses the relation as water erodes stone and torrents sweep soil away, setting retained water against destructive runoff.

basis: waters wear stone and wash away earth
note: Job makes flowing water an agent that erodes stone and carries soil away, a somber counterpart to the commentary's flood carrying scattered material off its surface.

basis: wadi streams dry up and vanish in heat
note: Job's unreliable watercourses disappear when heat comes, a close negative counterpart to the commentary's water held in pits and wells rather than lost with passing refuse.

basis: silver refined; Levites purified
note: The commentary's molten-metal foam separates from what can be used; Malachi depicts a refiner purifying silver and the Levites, giving separation of dross a priestly and ethical interpretation.

basis: refining and purifying silver for righteous offering
note: The refiner purifies the Levites like gold and silver so that their offering is righteous. This develops the commentary's molten-metal scene into a distinction between discarded impurity and enduring service.

basis: רַבִּים, abundant water from rock
note: The commentary explicitly labels its Arabic branch ر ب ب and glosses it as abundant water named for gathering; Numbers uses Hebrew מַיִם רַבִּים for abundant water gushing from the rock. The matching r-b-b form and water context suggest a cognate, though the source label alone does not establish it.

basis: singing to a well that springs up
note: Israel sings for a well to rise. The liturgical address to a spring offers a communal counterpart to the commentary's gathering water and its opening exhortation to praise the Lord.

basis: teaching of the wise as a fountain of life
note: The wise person's instruction is a life-giving fountain, joining the commentary's useful reminder to its well of plentiful, clear water.

basis: deep waters and a bubbling fountain of wisdom
note: The proverb calls human words deep waters and wisdom's fountain a flowing brook; it makes the word-water connection explicit without reducing the commentary's wells to a mere lexical cognate.

basis: muddied spring and polluted fountain
note: The commentary's source gloss describes cleaning a mud-covered well until clear water appears; Proverbs makes a muddied spring the image of a righteous person yielding to wickedness, giving the same water-clarity image an ethical force.

basis: dross removed from silver
note: The commentary includes foam on molten metal among the residue that separates from useful substance; Proverbs says removing dross from silver leaves material for the silversmith's vessel, a refining counterpart to foam departing while value remains.

basis: remove dross so a usable vessel emerges
note: Removing silver's dross produces a vessel for the refiner. This closely meets the commentary's furnace scene, where a surface waste separates from metal meant for useful objects.

basis: water-fed tree; enduring leaf
note: The commentary sets rain held in rock hollows against vegetation that dries into residue; Psalm 1's tree by irrigation channels bears fruit and does not wither, making lasting nourishment the counterpart to passing debris.

basis: tree by water bearing fruit
note: The one formed by instruction is a tree planted by water that continually yields fruit; it supplies the productive, life-giving side of water kept for benefit.

basis: chaff blown away
note: The commentary's Arabic غثاء is flood-borne plant residue that surfaces and disperses; Psalm 1 says the wicked are like chaff the wind drives away, making the discarded plant matter a moral image of what does not endure.

basis: chaff driven away
note: The wicked are like chaff the wind drives away, a precise land-based counterpart to the flood or pot refuse that is scattered, lost, and not retained.

basis: desert made pool and dry ground springs
note: The psalm reverses barrenness by making pools and springs from dry land, a direct water-gathering image alongside the commentary's flood-filled hollows.

basis: hungry people settle by the water
note: The next verse gives the human result of the new water: hungry people establish a habitation. It sharpens the commentary's phrase about what benefits people and remains.

basis: rock becomes pool and flint spring
note: The commentary describes God-created hollows in rock that collect rainwater; Psalm 114 says God turns rock into a pool and flint into a spring, adding the reversal in which rock itself becomes a source of provision.

basis: rock turned into a pool and flint into a spring
note: God makes hard rock a water pool and flint a fountain, directly matching the commentary's unusual attention to water gathered or appearing in rock.

basis: wicked removed like dross; statutes loved
note: The psalmist describes the wicked as dross removed from earth and responds by loving God's statutes, pairing discarded matter with enduring, valued instruction.

basis: precepts remembered because they give life
note: The psalmist vows never to forget God's precepts because through them God gives life. It directly joins the commentary's remembrance condition to demonstrable benefit.

basis: darkness cannot hide
note: The commentary says God knows the public and the hidden; the psalm says even darkness is not dark to God, making concealment itself no barrier to divine knowledge.

basis: waters roar and foam
note: The commentary distinguishes flood foam that disperses from water that remains; in the psalm's tumultuous scene the waters roar and foam as mountains shake, making foam part of threatening upheaval rather than a sign of useful water.

basis: garden fountain, living-water well, Lebanon streams
note: The Song joins a well of living water to abundant running streams and a garden, furnishing a rich biblical counterpart for the commentary's plentiful well and water-fed ground.

basis: fountain opened for cleansing
note: The commentary's well is cleared of mud until its water appears clean; Zechariah's opened fountain cleanses sin and impurity, turning clear water into a specific image of moral purification.

basis: fountain opened for cleansing
note: A fountain is opened to cleanse impurity; this provides a ritual analogue to the commentary's muddy well being cleared until its water appears and is clean.

basis: hope of immortality
note: The commentary calls the hereafter more abiding; Wisdom says the righteous may seem to die but their hope is full of immortality, explaining how apparent loss can conceal a lasting good.

basis: righteous tested like gold
note: The commentary's metal image separates passing foam from enduring value; Wisdom says God tests the righteous like gold in a furnace and accepts them, interpreting hardship as refinement rather than waste.

basis: wind-driven chaff, frost, smoke, and forgotten guest
note: The Wisdom writer depicts the impious hope as material blown or dispersed and as a guest's vanished memory. It closely illuminates the commentary's proverbial sense of refuse that disappears and is not reckoned with.
